blocks.text: Human fibroblasts grown in a dish divide about 40 to 60 times and then stop for good, even though nutrients are plentiful. A cell that has quietly counted its own divisions raises the question of what ageing is at the cellular level, and why a 30-year-old and an 80-year-old differ in how they handle the same illness.

blocks.markdown: Ageing is the progressive, time-dependent decline in cellular and organ function that increases vulnerability to disease and death. At the cellular level, it reflects **accumulated damage** to molecules and organelles together with a **programmed limit on replication**. Several mechanisms contribute and interact; none alone explains ageing.

blocks.title: Cellular senescence
blocks.text: Cellular senescence is the permanent arrest of the cell cycle in a cell that is still viable and metabolically active. Senescent cells do not respond to growth factors, are resistant to apoptosis, and often secrete inflammatory mediators.

blocks.markdown:
### Telomere shortening

**Telomeres** are repeated DNA sequences (TTAGGG in humans) with associated proteins that cap the ends of chromosomes, protecting them from being recognised as damaged DNA and from fusion. Because DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the extreme 3' end of the lagging strand (the **end-replication problem**), telomeres shorten with each cell division. When telomeres become critically short, the cell recognises them as DNA damage: p53 and p21 are activated and the cell enters **replicative senescence** (or apoptosis). This sets the **Hayflick limit** to the number of divisions of normal somatic cells.

Stem cells, germ cells and most cancers express **telomerase**, an enzyme that adds telomere repeats using an RNA template (TERC) and a catalytic protein (TERT). Most somatic cells have little or no telomerase. Reactivation of telomerase in cancer cells allows them to avoid senescence and divide without limit. Inherited defects of telomerase produce premature failure of high-turnover tissues such as bone marrow and lung (for example dyskeratosis congenita).

rows: Loss of repeats with each division; short telomeres trigger p53/p21
Reactive oxygen species and other agents cause mutations and breaks; repair becomes less efficient
Oxidative damage to proteins and lipids
Free radicals damage proteins and membranes; lipofuscin accumulates
Impaired chaperones, proteasome and autophagy, so misfolded proteins accumulate
Caloric restriction extends lifespan in animal models via reduced growth signalling (e.g. insulin/IGF-1, mTOR)
blocks.caption: Cellular mechanisms contributing to ageing.

blocks.title: How many divisions are left?
blocks.prompt: Telomeres in fibroblasts from a newborn average 10,000 base pairs. Each division loses about 100 bp, and replicative senescence begins at a critical length of 4,000 bp. Estimate the number of divisions available.

steps.text: Divisions = usable length / loss per division.
About 60 divisions, which is in line with the Hayflick limit observed in cultured fibroblasts.
A cell expressing telomerase replenishes the loss, so the arithmetic no longer applies and division can continue indefinitely.

blocks.answer: About 60 divisions, after which replicative senescence occurs; telomerase abolishes the limit.

blocks.markdown:
### Accumulated oxidative and DNA damage

Mitochondrial respiration generates **reactive oxygen species (ROS)**. Over decades, ROS damage lipids, proteins and DNA (including mitochondrial DNA, which lacks histone protection and has limited repair). Mitochondrial DNA mutations impair oxidative phosphorylation, which in turn raises ROS production. DNA damage from ROS, ultraviolet light and replication errors accumulates faster than repair can remove it, especially because repair capacity declines with age: this produces mutations, senescence and apoptosis. Insoluble oxidised protein and lipid complexes accumulate as **lipofuscin** ('wear and tear pigment') in long-lived cells such as neurons, cardiac myocytes and hepatocytes. Inherited defects in DNA repair cause accelerated ageing syndromes (for example Werner syndrome, caused by a defective DNA helicase).

blocks.title: Linking mechanisms
blocks.prompt: A 78-year-old has skin with many mutations from sun exposure, slow wound healing and numerous senescent fibroblasts. Connect these observations to cellular ageing mechanisms.

steps.text: Mutations: lifelong ultraviolet and oxidative DNA damage accumulates while repair declines.
Slow healing: fibroblast and keratinocyte replication has used up telomere length, so many cells are in replicative senescence and cannot proliferate to repair.
Senescent cells also secrete inflammatory mediators and matrix-degrading enzymes, further impairing tissue function.

blocks.answer: Cumulative DNA damage and telomere-driven senescence reduce regenerative capacity and raise cancer risk.

blocks.markdown:
### Normal ageing versus age-related disease

Ageing is not itself a disease. **Normal ageing** comprises gradual, universal, progressive changes that reduce reserve (for example slowly declining renal filtration, reduced skin elasticity, presbyopia, mild loss of muscle mass) but do not by themselves cause symptoms at rest. **Age-related disease** (atherosclerotic heart disease, osteoporosis fractures, dementia, cancer, osteoarthritis) is pathological, affects only some individuals and has specific lesions. Ageing is the strongest risk factor for many diseases because accumulated damage lowers resistance, but disease is not inevitable.

rows: Presbyopia, mild decline in renal filtration, skin thinning
Alzheimer disease, osteoporotic fracture, cancer, heart failure
blocks.caption: Normal ageing compared with age-related disease.

items: Telomerase is active in stem cells, germ cells and most cancers.
Senescent cells accumulate with age and secrete inflammatory factors.
Lipofuscin is a marker of cumulative oxidative damage.
Caloric restriction prolongs lifespan in experimental animals; this is not a clinical recommendation.

blocks.title: Damage plus limit
blocks.text: Cellular ageing combines a counting mechanism (telomere shortening leading to replicative senescence) with accumulated molecular damage (oxidative stress, DNA damage, protein misfolding). Their interaction explains why ageing raises both degenerative disease and cancer risk.

points: Telomeres shorten at each division until the DNA damage response (p53/p21) triggers replicative senescence; telomerase prevents this in stem cells and cancers.
Accumulating oxidative and DNA damage, mitochondrial dysfunction and defective protein homeostasis impair cell function with age.
Normal ageing is universal and gradual, whereas age-related diseases are specific pathological processes affecting some individuals.

questions.stem: Which enzyme adds telomere repeats and is active in stem cells and most cancers?
questions.explanation: Telomerase uses an RNA template to extend chromosome ends. Its absence in most somatic cells leads to telomere shortening.

questions.stem: Critically short telomeres cause replicative senescence mainly because:

options.text: They are recognised as DNA damage, activating p53 and p21 and halting the cell cycle

questions.correctOptionText: They are recognised as DNA damage, activating p53 and p21 and halting the cell cycle

distractorRationale.c: Telomerase is not activated in most somatic cells.

questions.explanation: Short telomeres expose chromosome ends, which trigger the DNA damage response and cell cycle arrest through p53 and p21. The cell remains alive but cannot divide.

questions.stem: A cancer cell line divides indefinitely in culture although its telomeres should have shortened. Which explanation is most likely?

options.text: Reactivation of telomerase maintains telomere length

questions.correctOptionText: Reactivation of telomerase maintains telomere length
questions.explanation: Most cancers express telomerase, which prevents telomere erosion and so removes the replicative limit.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of cellular ageing caused by accumulated oxidative damage?

options.text: Accumulation of lipofuscin in long-lived cells
Increased telomerase in all somatic cells

questions.correctOptionText: Accumulation of lipofuscin in long-lived cells

distractorRationale.b: Telomerase is low in somatic cells.

questions.explanation: Lipofuscin consists of insoluble oxidised lipid and protein, and builds up in neurons, myocytes and hepatocytes with age.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes normal ageing from age-related disease?

options.text: Normal ageing is universal and gradual and usually causes no symptoms at rest, whereas age-related disease affects only some people and has specific lesions
Age-related disease is inevitable in everyone

questions.correctOptionText: Normal ageing is universal and gradual and usually causes no symptoms at rest, whereas age-related disease affects only some people and has specific lesions
questions.explanation: Ageing is universal, gradual and reduces reserve, whereas diseases such as Alzheimer disease or osteoporosis are pathological and variable.

questions.stem: True or false: Mitochondrial DNA is especially vulnerable to oxidative damage because it lacks histone protection and has limited repair.
questions.explanation: Mitochondrial DNA lies close to the source of reactive oxygen species and is poorly protected. Mutations impair respiration and can increase ROS further.

questions.stem: Cultured keratinocytes have telomeres of 9,000 bp at the start of culture, lose 75 bp per division, and enter senescence at 3,000 bp. Calculate the expected number of divisions before senescence.
questions.explanation: Usable telomere length is 9000 - 3000 = 6000 bp, and 6000/75 = 80 divisions. If telomerase were expressed, the loss would be offset and the limit would not apply.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old has early bone marrow failure and pulmonary fibrosis, and his blood cells have unusually short telomeres due to an inherited telomerase defect. Which explanation best links the defect to these findings?

options.text: High-turnover tissues exhaust their replicative capacity early because telomeres cannot be maintained
Excessive telomerase activity causes uncontrolled division
Lipofuscin deposition blocks the bone marrow

questions.correctOptionText: High-turnover tissues exhaust their replicative capacity early because telomeres cannot be maintained

distractorRationale.b: The defect is loss, not excess, of telomerase.
distractorRationale.c: Lipofuscin is a wear pigment, not the mechanism.
distractorRationale.d: Short telomeres activate p53 rather than promoting its degradation.

questions.explanation: Without telomerase, stem and progenitor cells in rapidly renewing tissues reach critically short telomeres prematurely and undergo senescence or apoptosis. This produces premature failure of bone marrow and other tissues.

questions.stem: Describe the role of telomere shortening in cellular senescence and explain why telomerase expression matters in stem cells and cancer.
markingGuide: Telomeres cap chromosome ends; shorten with each division (end-replication problem)
Critically short telomeres signal DNA damage via p53 and p21
Cell cycle arrest: replicative senescence (Hayflick limit) or apoptosis
Telomerase (TERT/TERC) re-extends telomeres in stem cells and germ cells
Most cancers reactivate telomerase, achieving unlimited replication
questions.explanation: Telomere length acts as a mitotic counter. Telomerase overrides it, which benefits stem cells but also supports cancer immortality.

questions.stem: Explain how accumulated oxidative and DNA damage contribute to ageing, and distinguish normal age-related decline from age-related disease using two examples.
markingGuide: Mitochondrial ROS damage lipids, proteins and DNA including mtDNA
Declining repair leads to mutation, senescence and apoptosis
Normal ageing: universal, gradual, reduces reserve (e.g. presbyopia or slow decline in renal filtration)
Age-related disease: specific pathology affecting some (e.g. Alzheimer disease, osteoporotic fracture, cancer)
questions.explanation: Damage accumulates faster than repair, reducing cellular function. Normal ageing is a background change, whereas disease is a distinct pathological process.
